title: The Stoics
summary: Stoicism is a philosophical school that arose in Athens around 300 BC and flourished in Rome. Its central idea: we do not control events, but we can govern how we understand them and how we respond to them. The aim is to live “in accordance with nature” — that is, with reason, with integrity, and in connection with other people.
onEmotions: The Stoics distinguished “first movements” — involuntary bodily responses like trembling or tears, which are not in our power and for which no one is to blame — from “passions,” states in which we have already assented to a mistaken judgment such as “something terrible has happened.” The ideal was not numbness but apatheia — freedom from overwhelming passions — together with the eupatheiai, the good feelings: calm joy, reasonable caution, goodwill. For a Stoic, working with a feeling means carefully examining your own “impression”: what do I actually think about what is happening, and is it true?

anxiety.text: Anxiety is a natural response of a mind trying to protect you in advance from the unknown, and there is nothing shameful in it. The Stoics noticed, though, that anxiety is almost always aimed at the future — at what does not yet exist and what is mostly beyond our control. Epictetus considered one distinction the most important of all: our judgments, intentions and actions are up to us; other people's decisions, health, and the outcome of events are not. Anxiety often grows when we try to hold the second kind of thing in our hands. A Stoic doesn't ask you to stop feeling; he suggests gently sorting the worry: this part is mine, and I can do something about it today; this part is not mine, and I can let it go without ceasing to care about it. Then anxiety becomes not a verdict but a signal pointing to where your next step lies.
anxiety.practice: Write down what you are anxious about and divide the page into two columns: “up to me” and “not up to me.” Choose one small action from the first column.

quote.text: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the opinions about things.
quote.author: Epictetus

fear.text: Fear is an ancient protector, and the fact that it has switched on speaks of your ability to look after yourself and what you hold dear. Seneca wrote to his friend Lucilius that many things frighten us more than they can actually hurt us: imagination paints a disaster in every detail, though it hasn't happened yet and may never happen. The Stoics proposed an exercise later called “premeditatio malorum” — thinking through misfortunes in advance: calmly picture a difficult outcome and ask yourself what you would do and what strengths you could lean on. Paradoxically, looking straight at what frightens us often weakens its hold: a vague threat turns into a concrete difficulty that one can live with. Stoicism doesn't promise that there will be nothing left to fear. It reminds you that your capacity to meet whatever happens with dignity stays with you, whatever the outcome.
fear.practice: Name your fear in a single sentence, then ask yourself: “If this happens, what will I still have, and what will I be able to lean on?”

quote.text: There are more things likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
quote.author: Seneca

sadness.text: Sadness is a quiet feeling that often comes when something dear turns out differently than we hoped. The Stoics are sometimes imagined as people who forbade themselves to be sad, but that isn't quite right. Seneca acknowledged that the soul has “first movements” — an involuntary heaviness, tears — that are not in our power and need not be a source of shame. The Stoic work begins later: noticing what thought the sadness carries with it. Sometimes behind it is a simple “I'm sorry this happened,” and sometimes “everything will always be bad.” The first can simply be lived through; the second is worth checking, because it is already a judgment, and judgments are in our power. Marcus Aurelius often reminded himself that everything in the world flows and changes. This thought can be a comfort: your present state is also part of the flow, and it is not forever.
sadness.practice: Ask yourself: what thought accompanies my sadness? Write it down and note whether it is a fact or an assumption about the future.

grief.text: Loss is one of the hardest things a person can go through, and grief is love's natural response to the absence of someone we love. Seneca, who himself suffered many losses, wrote letters of consolation to his friends and did not demand stony calm from them. He allowed for tears, but advised not letting grief swallow the whole of life — and, above all, keeping in memory what had been given. The Stoics reminded us that everything dear to us is given not as our property but for a time — as if on loan from nature. The thought sounds stern, but it holds a comfort too: the time you spent together was real, and no one can take it away now. From the Stoic point of view, grieving is not weakness but the consequence of attachment, which the Stoics valued as well. Gradually, the pain can turn into grateful remembrance.
grief.practice: Recall one specific thing that the person you lost gave you — a word, a habit, a way of seeing the world. Write it down.

quote.text: Let not the eyes be dry when we have lost a friend, nor let them overflow.
quote.author: Seneca

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts because human beings are social by nature — and the Stoics fully agreed. They taught oikeiosis, “appropriation” or “making one's own”: from birth we reach toward caring for ourselves, and then this circle widens to include those close to us, our fellow citizens and, ideally, all of humanity. Marcus Aurelius wrote that we are made for working together, like feet, hands or eyelids. So your longing for closeness is not a weakness but the voice of human nature itself. At the same time, the Stoics valued being able to keep good company with oneself: Seneca advised spending time with the thoughts of worthy people, reading them as if in conversation. Loneliness can be taken as a reminder: I am part of a larger whole even when no one is nearby, and every kind thing I do is a thread tying me to others.
loneliness.practice: Think of one person you share some bond with, even a distant one. Consider what small kind act you could do for someone today.

anger.text: Anger often flares up when something important has been touched: fairness, your boundaries, your sense of dignity. Seneca devoted an entire treatise, On Anger, to this feeling and took the subject very seriously. He distinguished the first jolt — the rush of heat, the urge to respond, which arises on its own and for which you are not responsible — from what follows, when the mind assents to the thought “I have been wronged, and this must be repaid.” Seneca considered delay the best remedy for anger: anger weakens if you wait. Marcus Aurelius began his mornings by reminding himself that he would meet difficult people that day, that they act this way out of ignorance, and that he is nonetheless bound to them by a shared nature. From the Stoic point of view, you can accept anger as a signal about what you value — without rushing to hand it the wheel.
anger.practice: Before responding, pause for at least a few breaths and ask: “What matters so much to me here that this has touched me?”

quote.text: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
quote.author: Marcus Aurelius

shame.text: Shame is a feeling we want to hide, even though everyone experiences it. The Stoics help us look at it from another side. For Epictetus, a person's worth is determined not by the opinion of others, not by appearance, and not by success, but by how they use their prohairesis — the capacity to choose and to judge. Everything else the Stoics called “indifferent”: not trivial, but something that makes you neither a good nor a bad person. If your shame is tied to someone else's gaze, a Stoic would ask: is another person's opinion within my power? If shame points to something you did and regret, it is a sign that being decent matters to you — which means your capacity for good is intact. Epictetus reminded us that nothing great comes into being all at once: we learn all our lives.
shame.practice: Ask yourself: is my shame about what others will think of me, or about how I myself want to act? Write down one value it reveals to you.

guilt.text: Guilt tells you that you care how your actions affect others, and that in itself is a good sign. The Stoics regarded almost everyone as a prokopton, “one who is making progress” — a student on the way to wisdom, for whom mistakes are inevitable. Every evening Seneca reviewed the day he had lived: where did I act badly, what did I learn? Yet he stressed that he did this without cruelty toward himself — to understand, not to punish — and ended with words like “see that you do not do that again; this time I pardon you.” The past, according to the Stoics, is no longer in our power; what is in our power is what we do now: apologize, make amends, act differently next time. Guilt turned into such action has done its job. Guilt that gnaws endlessly no longer helps you or the people you hurt.
guilt.practice: In the evening, ask yourself as Seneca did: what went well today, what didn't, and what can I do differently tomorrow? End your review with words of forgiveness to yourself.

envy.text: Everyone knows envy: someone else's success suddenly stings inside, and that doesn't make you a bad person. Epictetus proposed a calm analysis. Everything has its price, he said: if someone was invited to a banquet and you weren't, it means he paid for the invitation — with flattery, time, effort. If you didn't pay that price, it's odd to demand the goods; but you still have what you kept. Moreover, for a Stoic the true good is virtue: wisdom, justice, courage, moderation — while wealth, fame and recognition are merely “preferred indifferents.” They are pleasant to have, but whether you live well does not depend on them. You can take envy as a hint about what you truly want — and ask what price you yourself are willing to pay for it.
envy.practice: Name exactly what you envy, and ask yourself: what price did the other person pay for this, and do I want to pay the same?

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy can come when your strength is gone and meaning seems lost — it is a heavy state, and you don't need to blame yourself for it. The Stoics didn't describe apathy in the modern sense: their word apatheia meant something else — freedom from overwhelming passions. But from a Stoic point of view, one can say that even in emptiness a person keeps a small foothold: the ability to choose how to relate to this moment. Marcus Aurelius admitted to himself that it was hard to get up in the morning, and reminded himself: I am rising to do the work of a human being. Not some great work — just the next one. The Stoics believed that everyone is connected to the common whole, the logos, the rational order of the world, and that even a small act of kindness or care brings us back into that connection. You don't have to find meaning all at once; you can make it little by little.
emptiness.practice: Choose one very small task for the next hour — pour a glass of water, open a window, write to someone — and do it, noticing that it is your choice.

confusion.text: Confusion arises when the familiar map of your life no longer matches the terrain. It is an honest state: you can see that the old answers don't fit. Epictetus began his Handbook — the Enchiridion, literally “that which is kept at hand” — with a single distinction: some things are in our power, others are not. When everything is mixed up, this distinction works like a compass. You don't need to understand the whole picture at once: it is enough to find what depends on you right now. Epictetus also spoke of “roles”: each of us is someone's son or daughter, friend, worker, citizen, and each role suggests what is fitting to do. Confusion can be accepted as a pause before a more precise choice. Better decisions are often born from it than from hasty certainty.
confusion.practice: Write down one thing that is definitely in your power right now, and one role you play in someone's life. What does that role suggest you do today?

fatigue.text: Fatigue and burnout are not a sign of weakness but a sign that you have been carrying a lot for a long time. The Stoics are often pictured as people of unbending will, but Seneca wrote that the mind needs rest like a field: without a break it becomes exhausted. He praised walks, a change of activity, friendly conversation, and even an unhurried meal shared with friends. Epictetus, in turn, helps us see where part of our tiredness may come from: we spend our strength on what is not in our power — on controlling other people's opinions, results, the future. Letting go of this is not giving up; it means no longer hauling a load that was never yours to begin with. From the Stoic point of view, conserving your strength is also part of living “in accordance with nature”: you are not a machine but a living being with limits, and respecting them is an expression of reason.
fatigue.practice: Recall what took the most energy today. Was it in your power? Allow yourself one short break without guilt.

boredom.text: Boredom seems like a small thing, but it can be agonizing: time drags and nothing brings joy. Seneca wrote a great deal about a similar state — a restless discontent in which people rush from place to place, travel, change occupations, while their inner irritation travels with them. You need to change your soul, not the sky above you, he replied to a friend who complained that his journeys did not help. From a Stoic point of view, boredom may suggest that your attention has drifted into waiting for something external to entertain you. The Stoics proposed bringing attention back to the present: Marcus Aurelius advised doing each task wholly, fully present, without being distracted by busyness. You can take boredom as an invitation: notice what is happening right now, and ask what this time might serve.
boredom.practice: Choose one ordinary action — washing a cup, taking a walk — and do it with full attention, as if seeing it for the first time. What did you notice?

joy.text: Joy is a wonderful feeling, and the Stoics were by no means against it. On the contrary, among the eupatheiai, the good feelings of the sage, joy was named first — chara in Greek, gaudium in Latin. Seneca wrote to Lucilius that true joy is a serious matter: it grows from within, from a good life, rather than depending on fortune's chance gifts. The Stoics distinguished this deep joy from fleeting pleasure, which disappears along with its external cause. That doesn't mean you can't be glad of external things: you can, just without clutching them in a death grip. From the Stoic point of view, your joy is especially steady when it is connected with what you did, what you understood, how you treated others — with what no one can take away.
joy.practice: Recall something that made you glad today. What part of that joy is connected with your own attitude or action?

quote.text: Above all, my dear Lucilius, make this your business: learn how to feel joy.
quote.author: Seneca

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the most human of feelings, and the Stoics, despite their stern image, valued them. They considered attachment to family and friends natural: it is the same oikeiosis, care that widens from oneself to those close to us. Epictetus did, admittedly, give a difficult piece of advice: when you embrace someone you love, remember that they are mortal and not given to you forever. It sounds cold, but the point is different — such remembrance makes tenderness more alive and attentive, guarding against the habit of taking loved ones for granted. Seneca called friendship a great good and wrote that the wise person seeks a friend not for advantage, but so as to have someone to care for and stand by. From the Stoic point of view, love is purest when it holds more wishing well for the other than wishing to possess.
love.practice: Think of one person close to you and what you value in them right now. You could tell them — or simply stay with that thought for a while.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a feeling the Stoics cultivated deliberately. The first book of Marcus Aurelius's Meditations consists entirely of thanks: to his grandfather, his mother, his teachers, his friends — to each for a specific quality or lesson he received from them. The emperor who ruled a vast realm began his private notes not with his worries but with a list of what others had given him. Seneca wrote a treatise, On Benefits, and considered ingratitude one of the most widespread vices, while the ability to receive good and remember it was a sign of a healthy soul. From the Stoic point of view, gratitude restores our sense of connection with the whole: we did not make ourselves. It also helps with acceptance: even on a hard day you can find what was given, and it balances what was taken away.
gratitude.practice: Like Marcus Aurelius, write one line in the form “From … — …”: from whom, and what quality or lesson you received.

hope.text: Hope helps us hold on, and in hard times it is especially precious. The Stoics' attitude toward it, however, is complicated, and it is only honest to show it. Seneca quoted the philosopher Hecato's saying that hope and fear go hand in hand. He meant that they are two sides of one state: a mind suspended over a future that does not depend on us. This is not a call to despair — quite the opposite. The Stoics proposed moving our footing from the future into the present: not “everything will surely be fine,” but “whatever happens, I will try to meet it with dignity.” Such hope in yourself, in your ability to respond, is sturdier than hope in circumstances. You can go on hoping for good things — just without making your inner steadiness wholly dependent on the outcome.
hope.practice: Complete the sentence: “I hope that… — and whatever happens, I can…” Pay attention to the second part.

quote.text: You will cease to fear if you cease to hope.
quote.author: Seneca (quoting Hecato)

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a sweet and slightly sad longing for the past, and there is a lot of love in it for what you have lived. The Stoics help us see in it more than loss. In his treatise On the Shortness of Life, Seneca wrote that the past is the most secure part of our life: it is already beyond fortune's reach, and it cannot be taken away. What was good will forever remain as having been. At the same time, Marcus Aurelius constantly reminded himself that we can live only in the present — the only time we truly have. From the Stoic point of view, nostalgia can be accepted as a grateful remembrance that nourishes, rather than an attempt to bring back what cannot return. The past becomes not a place you want to escape to, but a store from which you draw strength and an understanding of what you hold dear.
nostalgia.practice: Recall a moment from the past that you miss. What exactly was valuable in it — and does that value have a place in your life now?

craving.text: A craving — that sharp “I want it right now” — feels almost like an order, and there is nothing shameful in its being strong. The Stoics described in detail a mechanism very much like it. First comes an “impression” — a picture of relief, of taste, of calm. Then the mind either gives it “assent” (synkatathesis in Greek) or does not. Epictetus advised not assenting right away, but saying to the impression something like: “Wait, let me look at what you are.” Between impulse and action there is a gap, and your freedom lives in it. The craving itself may not disappear — the Stoics didn't demand that you not feel it; they suggested not confusing a sensation with a command. Every wave you have waited out is practice, not an exam, and its outcome does not determine your worth.
craving.practice: When the craving rolls in, say to it in your mind: “Wait, let me look at you” — and notice what exactly it promises: relief, rest, warmth, forgetting?

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure but a loop that took a long time to form and holds on tight. The Stoics thought a great deal about habit. Epictetus observed that every capacity is strengthened by the corresponding actions: walking by walking, running by running. So the loop of addiction is something that has been trained many times over, not your “nature” — and in the same way, step by step, something else can be trained. Epictetus, himself a former slave, considered freedom the chief business of philosophy: free is the one whose “ruling part,” the hegemonikon, has not been handed over to the power of things. At the same time, the Stoics spoke with respect of the prokoptontes, “those making progress” — people on the way rather than at the goal. In this picture, setbacks do not cancel the path. Even Seneca wrote his letters to Lucilius as a fellow traveler, not as a mentor who had already overcome everything.
addiction.practice: Recall one day or hour when the loop loosened even a little. What helped then? If you'd like, you can talk about it with someone who understands — for example, in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: The morning after can be doubly hard: the body aches, and your head swirls with anxiety, shame, fragments of last night. Many people know this, and such a morning deserves not a verdict but gentleness. The Stoics distinguished “first movements” — the body's involuntary response: trembling, heaviness, turmoil — from the judgments we add on top: “I'm awful,” “everything is ruined.” The first simply needs to be waited out while you take care of yourself. The second can be examined. Marcus Aurelius advised separating the bare event from the evaluation: “this is what happened” — without writing a verdict onto it. Seneca told how every evening he reviewed the day that had passed, asking himself without self-flagellation: what did I do wrong, what can be put right? Yesterday is no longer in your power; your response to it today is.
hangover.practice: In one column write the facts about yesterday, and in another the judgments that have stuck to them. Is there one small thing you can calmly do today?

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is vivid, and there can be a lot that is real in it: a taste for life, a sense of strength and possibility. There's no need to spoil it with suspicion. The Stoics distinguished the “passion” of pleasure — an excitement resting on the thought “this is the most important thing, I need more of it” — from the eupatheia of joy, which is calm and rests on what is within us. You might say that a Stoic doesn't extinguish the high but asks it a small question: what are you resting on? If on something external — luck, praise, an event — then, like everything external, the high will come and go. Marcus Aurelius constantly reminded himself that everything flows and changes. Here that thought doesn't cool things down but sets you free: you can enjoy without clutching and without promising yourself it will always be like this. Then the way down will be gentler too.
euphoria.practice: In the middle of the high, pause for three breaths and name exactly what you are glad about. Write it down — it will come in handy when the wave recedes.

crash.text: The drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a vivid evening — can be unexpectedly steep, and it is not your fault: this is often how waves work. The Stoics would say the comedown is especially painful because of an involuntary comparison: “yesterday was like that, and today is like this — so something must be broken.” But both yesterday's high and today's low belong to the “external” — to what comes and goes. Marcus Aurelius looked at life as a stream of changes and saw in it not a threat but the natural order of things. The Stoic foothold is not mood, but what you can do and how you relate to what is happening. Even on a gray day, small things remain within reach: doing one task honestly, being kind to someone — yourself included. The low is part of the flow too, and it will pass as well.
crash.practice: Ask yourself: “What in today still depends on me?” Choose one very small task and do it.

panic.text: A wave of panic is truly frightening: your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, it seems something irreparable is about to happen. Going through this is very hard, and it is not your fault that it happens. The Stoics knew that the body can respond before reason does — they called these “first movements”: trembling, pallor, ragged breathing come without our consent, and not even the sage is immune to them. There is comfort in this: the wave itself is not your failure. The Stoic part of the work is gently not adding a second layer of judgments like “this will never end.” A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. You can meet it like bad weather: not arguing with it, but anchoring yourself in the present moment — the only one, as Marcus Aurelius wrote, that we actually have.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor, feel the support beneath you, and take a few breaths with the exhale longer than the inhale. Silently name five objects you can see.

dread.text: Existential dread — “what's the point of all this,” the thought of our finitude — can come over you suddenly, and it speaks of the depth of your mind, not of weakness. The Stoics did not turn away from these questions. Marcus Aurelius often thought about the fleetingness of everything — and drew from it not the conclusion that nothing matters, but that the present is precious: since time is limited, each day can be lived attentively and kindly. For the Stoics, meaning lies not somewhere outside, in a guarantee of eternity, but in the very way of living — with reason, justly, in connection with others. Marcus wrote that people are made for working together, like hands, feet or eyelids. The abyss doesn't vanish because of this, but beside it a foothold appears: this day, this person, this good deed. That is enough to keep going.
dread.practice: Write down one person or one task that is dear to you today. Stay with that thought for a minute.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living a more interesting life and you're not where you should be is very common — especially when other people's lives are visible around the clock in your feed. Epictetus has a sober image for this: the banquet. Behave in life as at a banquet: a dish reaches you — take a moderate portion; it passes by — don't hold it back; it hasn't reached you yet — don't stretch for it from afar, wait. Epictetus also reminded us that everything has its price: someone was invited to the party because they paid for the invitation with time, flattery, effort — and you kept something of your own. From this point of view you are “where you should be,” at least in one sense: only here do you have access to what depends on you. Someone else's feast doesn't cancel your own table.
fomo.practice: When “I'm missing out” stings, ask: “What dish is in front of me right now?” Name one thing in this day that you can give your real attention to.

sleepless.text: At night, at three in the morning, thoughts have a way of becoming louder and darker than in the daytime — very many people know this. In one of his letters Seneca tells how he lived right above a noisy bathhouse, and reflects that outer quiet brings no peace if there is unrest within. The Stoics would suggest not settling big questions at night: judgments born in darkness and fatigue are worth postponing until morning and examining in daylight. Seneca wrote that every evening he reviewed the day that had passed and then let it go — and that sleep after such a review is more peaceful. You don't have to argue with every nighttime thought. You can politely tell it, “I'll hear you out tomorrow,” and return to your breathing. In the morning many of these thoughts will turn out smaller than they seemed.
sleepless.practice: If a thought won't let go, write it on a slip of paper by your bed with the note “will sort out in the morning.” Set the paper down and return to your breathing.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds especially deeply because it comes from where you placed your trust. Your pain makes sense, and the Stoics don't suggest pretending nothing happened. Marcus Aurelius knew treachery firsthand: his general Avidius Cassius raised a rebellion against him. In the Meditations Marcus reminds himself again and again that people act badly because they are mistaken about good and evil — and that this is their error, not a measure of your worth. Another person's act cannot make you worse: how you respond remains in your power. At the same time, a Stoic is not obliged to trust again someone who betrayed them — reasonable caution is also one of the eupatheiai, the good feelings. You can grieve the lost trust, protect yourself, and not let bitterness take over everything, all at the same time.
betrayal.practice: Write down: “What does this act say about them?” — and separately: “What remains mine, no matter what?” Compare the two lists.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is a mixture of fear of loss, pain and insecurity, and behind it lies an attachment that is precious to you. The Stoics would say jealousy is agonizing also because it is aimed at what by its very nature is not in our power: another person's feelings and choices. Epictetus reminded us that those close to us are not given to us as property, and advised never to say of anything “I have lost it,” but rather “I have given it back.” That sounds stern, but there is relief in it too: you don't need to — and can't — control another person. What is in your power is something else: being honest, speaking about your feelings, caring for the relationship and for yourself. You might say that Stoic love is not possession but attentive presence beside a free human being.
jealousy.practice: On a sheet of paper, separate what you know for certain in this situation from what your imagination is filling in. What one honest step or conversation is in your power?

resentment.text: An old grudge you carry around with you is heavy, and behind it there is usually a real injustice. The Stoics would take it seriously — and would also ask: whom is it hurting more right now? In On Anger, Seneca shows how resentment grows when we retell ourselves the insult again and again, adding ever new interpretations to the fact. Marcus Aurelius wrote that the best way to defend yourself against someone who wronged you is not to become like them. Letting go of resentment doesn't mean saying “everything was fine,” or necessarily making peace. It means taking back the part of your attention that for years has gone into an old wound. Your judgment of what they did may stay the same — all that leaves is the endless rumination that torments you most of all.
resentment.practice: Ask yourself: “What does this resentment want me finally to acknowledge?” Write down the answer — sometimes a grudge just needs to be heard.

heartbreak.text: A breakup turns life upside down: habits, plans, the voice beside you all disappear. A broken heart truly hurts, and the Stoics recognized such “first movements” as natural. Consoling his friends, Seneca advised not forbidding yourself to grieve, but also not making grief the only content of your life. The Stoic view suggests holding two things together. The first: what was between you was real — Seneca wrote that the past is safe, and no one can take it away now. The second: the other person is free, and their choice is not a verdict on you. Your worth isn't decided by whether this love stayed with you. Gradually you can take back what is yours — friendships, work, caring for yourself — without hurrying the pain.
heartbreak.practice: Write down one thing you took from this relationship and want to keep. And one thing you would like to bring back into your life now.

impostor.text: The fear that “I'm about to be found out” is familiar to many capable people, and your very demandingness toward yourself speaks of conscientiousness. The Stoics would shift the question. Epictetus placed other people's opinions, reputation and recognition among the things “not in our power.” What is in our power is how we do our work: honestly, attentively. Epictetus even advised: if you want to make progress, be content to seem ignorant in external matters. The Stoics did not pretend to be sages — they called themselves “those making progress” and saw nothing shameful in it. You don't have to know everything already. Being a student of your craft is not a deception but an honest position, and there is no need to hide it.
impostor.practice: Write down one thing you did conscientiously today, whether or not anyone noticed. And one thing you want to learn.

self_hatred.text: If your inner critic sounds harsh and merciless, that is very hard, and you deserve support, not yet another verdict. The Stoics are sometimes imagined as stern judges of themselves, but their self-examination was different. Seneca described his evening review of the day as a conversation in which he said to himself: “see that you don't do that again; this time I pardon you.” He examined actions; he did not pass sentence on his whole person. In the Meditations, Marcus Aurelius also talks to himself — demandingly, but as to a friend: if something didn't work out, don't despair; come back to it again. From the Stoic point of view, the voice insisting “I'm worthless” is not reason but a passion — that is, a mistaken judgment — and you are not at all obliged to agree with it.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one phrase from your inner critic and rewrite it the way Seneca would speak to a friend: about a specific action, with forgiveness, and with one step forward.

helplessness.text: Helplessness is one of the most tormenting feelings: it seems nothing can be changed. The Stoics didn't deny that a huge part of life is not in our power — on the contrary, that is exactly where they began. But their distinction works in both directions. Even when circumstances don't depend on you, a thin but real area remains: how you understand what is happening, where you direct your attention, how you treat yourself and others. Epictetus, a former slave who was also lame, knew powerlessness firsthand — and perhaps that is exactly why he so valued this small island of freedom. Helplessness before the large does not cancel strength in the small. Sometimes the only thing you can do is live today gently. That is already a lot.
helplessness.practice: Write down what in this situation is definitely not in your power — and, separately, one tiny thing that is still yours.

quote.text: Some things are under our control, while others are not under our control.
quote.author: Epictetus

procrastination.text: “I can't get started” is not laziness or a flaw of character; often fear, fatigue, or a task that is simply too big lies behind it. Seneca opens his letters to Lucilius with precisely the theme of time: most of it slips away unnoticed while we postpone, and every day we have lived already belongs to the past. But the Stoics didn't say this to shame anyone. Marcus Aurelius, judging by his notes, also found it hard to get up in the morning and coaxed himself: I am rising to do the work of a human being. The Stoic solution is to focus not on the whole task but on the next action: do what is in front of you as if it were the only thing. To begin means to take a very small first step, not to conquer everything at once.
procrastination.practice: Pick the smallest piece of the task — five minutes' worth. Tell yourself, as Marcus Aurelius did in the morning, “I'm doing this because it is my work,” and start only that piece.

quote.text: Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time.
quote.author: Seneca

uprooted.text: Being torn away from home means losing not only an address but the language of the streets, familiar faces, the feeling of ground beneath your feet. It is real grief. The Stoics knew it from the inside: Seneca spent eight years in exile on Corsica, and Musonius Rufus and Epictetus were also banished from Rome. In the consolation he wrote to his mother from exile, Seneca said that wherever we are cast, the nature we all share and our own soul remain with us. The Stoics called themselves “cosmopolitans” — citizens of the world: a person belongs not only to their own city but to the vast community of all human beings. This doesn't cancel homesickness, but it offers a second foothold: you haven't fallen out of the world, you are in another part of it, and here too there are people you can grow close to.
uprooted.practice: Name one thing you brought with you on the inside — a habit, a language, a skill. And one person nearby you could talk with, even a little.

overload.text: When the feed never ends, and there are more news stories, messages and other people's opinions than your head can hold, fatigue and irritation are natural. Seneca wrote about something similar: in his second letter to Lucilius he warns that reading many authors haphazardly scatters the mind — whoever is everywhere is, in effect, nowhere; better a few things, but thoroughly. Epictetus advised testing every “impression” before letting it in: what are you, and do you concern me? And Marcus Aurelius observed that most of what we say and do is not necessary, and advised asking ourselves before each of them: is this needed? The Stoic filter is simple: most of the noise is not in your power and does not require your assent.
overload.practice: Before opening the next news story or feed, ask yourself Marcus Aurelius's question: “Is this necessary?” If not, put it off for ten minutes.

unreality.text: Sometimes there is a feeling that everything around you — or you yourself — isn't quite real, as if behind glass. It's a strange and often unsettling experience, and it can be talked about calmly. The Stoics didn't describe it in modern terms, but from a Stoic point of view one can say that the foothold in such moments lies not in understanding at once what is happening, but in what is always close at hand: the body, the present moment, the next task. Marcus Aurelius liked to describe things with utmost concreteness, “as they are”: this purple robe is sheep's wool dyed with shellfish blood; this wine is grape juice. Such sober naming can help restore contact: here is the table, here is the cup, here is my hand. The world hasn't gone anywhere, and you can return to it step by step.
unreality.practice: Silently name five simple things around you, describing them concretely as Marcus Aurelius did: color, material, shape. Feel your feet touching the floor.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful — a starry sky, the sea, music — is one of the deepest human experiences, and the Stoics valued it highly. For them the world is a single living order, pervaded by logos, the rational principle, and the human being is part of it. Marcus Aurelius advised rising in thought and looking at human affairs from above: this “view from above” makes small worries smaller and the connection with the whole more tangible. Seneca wrote that contemplating nature lifts up the soul and leads it out of the cramped quarters of everyday cares. For a Stoic, reverence is not an escape from life but a reminder of its scale: you are a small but real part of a vast whole. This feeling can simply be lived, without hurrying to explain it.
awe.practice: When awe takes hold of you, stay in it for a minute. Then ask yourself: how does today's worry look against this?

relief.text: Relief is a warm wave when tension lets go, and it's pleasant simply to live through it. The Stoics would say relief often shows how much strength went into waiting for disaster: Seneca noted more than once that imagination torments us more than events themselves. Relief is a good moment to see this without reproach: “so that's how much I was carrying.” The Stoics also valued gratitude that things turned out all right — not as a duty, but as a natural continuation of relief. You might also notice that the difficulty you went through left you something: experience, knowledge of your own strength. Epictetus said it is precisely difficulties that show what a person is. And for now, you can simply breathe out and allow yourself to rest.
relief.practice: Take a long exhale and tell yourself: “That's behind me.” Then write down what helped you endure the waiting.

calm.text: Calm is a precious state, and the Stoics considered it one of the fruits of philosophy. They called it euthymia — good-heartedness, an even disposition of mind; Seneca devoted a whole treatise to it, On Tranquility of Mind. Stoic calm is not the absence of events but steadiness within, when you are not dependent on every wave outside. Marcus Aurelius wrote that people seek retreats in the country, by the sea, in the mountains, but at any moment you can withdraw into yourself. The calm you feel now is exactly an experience of such an inner refuge. It's worth remembering it with your body: how your breath, your shoulders, your gaze feel. Then on a hard day you'll have somewhere to return to.
calm.practice: Notice where in your body calm is felt right now. Remember that place — you can return to it in your mind later.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a lively surge when you want to act and create, and it is joyful in itself. The Stoics would say it reveals the rational nature of the human being, which strives toward action: Marcus Aurelius reminded himself that a person is born for work, not for lying snug under the blankets. Seneca constantly stressed that philosophy is tested by deeds, not fine words, and advised Lucilius to turn good thoughts into practice. The Stoic advice to someone inspired is simple: let the impulse become action, even a small one — and don't make it a condition that inspiration last forever. Work begun on the upswing can be calmly continued when the upswing subsides.
inspiration.practice: Write down the idea that inspires you and immediately take a small first step — a sketch, a note, one email.

quote.text: Philosophy teaches us to act, not to speak.
quote.author: Seneca

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is a feeling people rarely admit to, but almost everyone knows it, and its appearance doesn't make you a bad person. The Stoics would explain it through the “impression”: somewhere inside, you assented to the thought that someone else's failure adds something to you — justice, room, relief from rivalry. Epictetus would object: a person's good lies in their own choice, their prohairesis, so another's failure adds nothing to your good and takes nothing away. Marcus Aurelius wrote that people are born for working together, like the hands and feet of one body, and that working against one another is contrary to nature. From this point of view, schadenfreude can be seen as a signal: somewhere you feel shortchanged or hurt. That is exactly the place worth looking at — gently, without self-reproach.
schadenfreude.practice: When you notice schadenfreude, ask yourself: “What do I feel I gain from this failure?” Write the answer in one sentence.

contempt.text: Contempt is a cold feeling: a person seems to become smaller in your eyes. Often fatigue, hurt, or a wish to protect yourself lies behind it. The Stoics themselves advised “despising” many things — fame, luxury, the opinion of the crowd — that is, seeing that these don't make a person better. But toward people themselves, Marcus Aurelius took a different attitude: someone who errs does so out of ignorance of what is good and what is bad, and yet remains your kin in reason. Epictetus proposed a simple exercise: if someone drinks a lot of wine, don't say “badly,” say “a lot”; how do you know why he does it? From the Stoic point of view, contempt is a judgment, not a fact. You can notice it and split it in two: what the person actually did — and what verdict I added to it.
contempt.practice: Describe the act that stirs your contempt dryly, as in an official report — without evaluative words. Notice whether the feeling changes.

disgust.text: Disgust is an ancient bodily feeling that makes us recoil from what seems dirty, alien or spoiled; it can concern people, situations, and even ourselves. The Stoics knew how strongly the “impression” shapes it. Marcus Aurelius practiced describing things “as they are,” stripping them of their aura: purple is wool dyed with a shellfish's blood. But he also noticed the reverse: to one who looks into nature, even the cracks in bread, the foam at a lion's mouth, and the wrinkles of old age have their own charm (III, 2). From the Stoic point of view, disgust can be respected as a protection, but not taken as the last word: what provokes it is also part of nature, with its own order. And if disgust is turned on yourself, a Stoic would remind you: neither your body nor your mistakes exhaust who you are — what matters most in you is the capacity to judge and to choose.
disgust.practice: Describe what disgusts you in neutral words, like a naturalist. What changes when the evaluative adjectives drop away?

revenge.text: The desire for revenge is a natural response to pain inflicted on you: it carries a sense of justice and a need for your pain to be acknowledged. In On Anger, Seneca examined exactly this thirst for retribution and considered it the most destructive part of anger: revenge makes us serve the one who hurt us — think about them, spend our time and strength on them. From the Stoic point of view, the wish for revenge is at first only a “first movement,” and you are not responsible for its arising; but you decide whether to assent to the thought “I must pay them back.” You can acknowledge: I'm hurting, I was treated unfairly — and direct your strength toward protecting yourself and your boundaries rather than toward harming someone else. That way you remain the master of your own life, not an extension of someone else's act.
revenge.practice: Write down what acknowledgment or what protection you would really like. Is there one calm step toward it that harms no one?

quote.text: The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong doer.
quote.author: Marcus Aurelius

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to you is especially painful: you love someone — and suddenly you're boiling, and afterward you feel ashamed. This is very human: with the people closest to us we are least defended. Epictetus offered an image: everything has two handles, by one of which it can be carried and by the other not. If your brother wrongs you, don't take hold of the handle “he has wronged me” — it cannot be carried that way; take hold of the other: “he is my brother, we were brought up together” (Enchiridion, 43). This doesn't cancel your anger — it may point to an important need. Every evening Seneca reviewed the day that had passed, calmly and without self-flagellation: where did I flare up, what touched a nerve, how will I act differently? From the Stoic point of view, an outburst doesn't cancel love; it shows the spot where a pause is needed next time.
anger_at_loved.practice: In the evening, recall one outburst and ask yourself, as Seneca did: what touched a nerve? How do I want to respond next time? No verdict on yourself.

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and at the same time not being able to stand them is one of the most tangled states there is, and it happens far more often than people usually admit. The Stoics would help untangle this knot. For them, a person close to you is not wholly “good” or wholly “bad,” but a living human being, with actions in their own power and traits you don't get to choose. The late Stoic Hierocles described our life as a system of circles — myself, my family, my relatives, fellow citizens, all of humanity — and considered it our task to draw these circles closer toward the center. For the Stoics, the bond with those close to us is not only a feeling but a chosen attitude. From a Stoic point of view, you don't have to demand of yourself a whole, uniform love: it is enough to distinguish what exactly stirs tenderness and what stirs irritation, and to respond to each separately.
ambivalence.practice: Divide a page into two columns: “what I value in them” and “what I find hard to bear.” Just look at how both columns exist at once.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, a departure, or even the death of a loved one who was ill for a long time is a feeling many people secretly blame themselves for. But relief and love can live side by side. A long heaviness — caregiving, fear, powerlessness — wears a person down, and when it ends, body and mind naturally breathe out. From the Stoic point of view, this is a “first movement,” not a verdict on your love. In his letters of consolation, Seneca did not demand uniform sorrow and advised that, in time, we remember those who are gone with joy and not only with anguish (Letter LXIII). Epictetus would remind you: you are answerable for how you acted, not for which feeling rose up on its own. Relief speaks of how hard it was — not of your having loved less.
guilty_relief.practice: Write yourself one sentence: “I feel lighter because it was very hard.” Notice that this is true — and that the love hasn't vanished because of it.

indifference.text: Sometimes something ought to move you — someone else's misfortune, an event, important news — and yet inside it's quiet. That can be frightening: “Is something wrong with me?” The Stoics are often pictured as preachers of unfeelingness, but that isn't accurate: their apatheia is not indifference but freedom from overwhelming passions, alongside a living care for others. From a Stoic point of view, one could say that a lull sometimes comes after long overstrain, like silence after noise, and in itself says nothing about your kindness. What the Stoics considered most important was not the strength of a feeling but intention and action: in On Benefits, Seneca wrote that the value of a good deed lies in the will of the one who does it. You can care even when emotion is silent. The feeling may come back later, and for now action is enough.
indifference.practice: Choose one small kind act that requires no special feelings: write to someone, call, help. Do it — and simply note that you did.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything and leave — change your job, your city, your role — is familiar to many, especially when the load has long been more than you can bear. Seneca treated this impulse with sympathy, but also with a question. In one of his letters to Lucilius (XXVIII) he recalls Socrates' reply to a man whom travel did not help: why be surprised, if you take yourself along wherever you go? The point is not that you mustn't leave, but that part of the weight travels with us. Seneca suggested sorting it out: what exactly am I running from — the place, or the way I live in it? Epictetus would add: look at what here is in your power. Sometimes a change is a sensible choice; sometimes it is enough to change the inner order of things. The urge to get away is not weakness but an honest signal that something needs to change.
escape.practice: Complete the sentence: “I want to get away from…” — and list everything. Mark which of it is tied to the place and which will travel with you.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is unavailable or “not the right one” can be confusing and unsettling: the feeling arises on its own without asking permission. The Stoics help lift some of the guilt from it. Attraction itself is a “first movement,” an impression that comes without our consent; Epictetus taught that which “impressions” come to us is not in our power, but how we deal with them is. He advised not hurrying, and saying to the impression: wait, let me see what you are and what you are about (Discourses, II, 18). From a Stoic point of view, you can ask: what exactly draws me — the person themselves, or what they represent for me: freedom, attention, a different life? Such a question passes no verdicts and commands nothing; it simply gives you back clarity and the right to decide for yourself.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Ask yourself: what quality or what possibility does this person embody for me? Write down one word.

social_anxiety.text: Shyness and fear of judgment are among the most common experiences: when people are looking at you, it feels as if you are being weighed. Epictetus, a former slave, thought a great deal about other people's opinions and considered them the prime example of what is “not in our power”: what others think of you is up to them. It sounds like bad news, but there is freedom in it — you can stop being responsible for what goes on in other people's heads. He even advised: if you want to make progress, be content to be thought ignorant in external matters (Enchiridion, 13). Marcus Aurelius marveled that each of us loves ourselves more than anyone, yet values others' opinion of us above our own (XII, 4). From the Stoic point of view, your task in a conversation is to be honest and kind; the impression you make is no longer your job.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, choose one intention within your power — for example, “to listen attentively.” Afterward, ask yourself only about that, not about how you came across.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is exhausting: the mind wants to know how everything will end, and there is no answer. The Stoics lived in a world where war, exile or illness could come at any moment — and they developed a particular attitude toward this. They advised acting “with a reserve clause”: intend, do everything you can, and add to yourself, “if nothing prevents it.” Such action doesn't depend on the outcome: your part is done even if the result turns out differently. Marcus Aurelius suggested not troubling yourself by picturing your whole life at once, but asking what in the present moment is truly unbearable (VIII, 36). From a Stoic point of view, uncertainty is not a malfunction but the ordinary state of the world; your support comes not from knowing the future, but from clarity about how you will respond to whatever comes.
uncertainty.practice: Write down one intention for the next few days and add to it: “…if nothing prevents it.” Notice how the feeling changes.

waiting.text: Waiting for results, an answer or news can be more agonizing than the news itself: life seems to be put on pause. Seneca knew this state well and wrote about it in On the Shortness of Life: expectation hanging on tomorrow robs us of today. The Stoics didn't suggest you stop waiting — that's impossible — but they suggested a distinction: the outcome is in other hands, but how you live today is up to you. Epictetus would say: the letter will come or not regardless of how many times you check your phone; but this evening, a conversation with a friend, a walk — those are yours. From a Stoic point of view, waiting can be accepted as a background, without handing it all your time. Waiting and living at the same time is a skill too, and one you can learn.
waiting.practice: Name one task for today that doesn't depend on the answer you're waiting for, and do it wholeheartedly, without checking for news.

quote.text: The greatest obstacle to living is expectancy, which hangs upon tomorrow and loses today.
quote.author: Seneca

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn't do is a sign that you care how you live. The Stoics looked at the past soberly: it is no longer in our power, and it can't be changed. Marcus Aurelius reminded himself that each of us lives only in the present instant, and the rest is either already lived or unknown (III, 10). But this is not a call to forget. Seneca reviewed each day every evening and admitted that he did so without fear, since he could say to himself: “See that you don't do that again; this time I pardon you” (On Anger, III, 36). From the Stoic point of view, regret is useful when it becomes a lesson, and tormenting when it becomes a verdict. The past can be turned into understanding, and understanding into your next action.
regret.practice: Write down what you regret, and next to it one thing this regret teaches you to do differently. End with Seneca's words: “This time I pardon you.”

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is a feeling that general words can hardly console. The Stoics didn't consider it a weakness. Seneca wrote to Lucilius about how his friend's letters delighted him: they bring real traces, real marks of the absent friend, a hand one recognizes (Letter XL). He believed that closeness can be kept in our thoughts: a friend we think of is, in a sense, with us. At the same time, the Stoics reminded us that the people we love are not in our power and are not given to us forever. The thought is bitter, but it teaches us to treasure every meeting and every letter. From a Stoic point of view, longing speaks of the value of a bond; you can allow it to be, and at the same time sustain that bond — with a word, a memory, something you would have done together.
longing.practice: Write this person a few lines — even if you don't send them. Or recall one shared moment in every detail.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — heavy news, wars, injustice — is natural for a sensitive person; it isn't weakness but a sign that you feel your connection with others. The Stoics called the human being a “cosmopolitan,” a citizen of the world: we belong not only to our own city but to all of humanity. Marcus Aurelius wrote his Meditations during wars and an epidemic, and much of it is about how not to grow hardened. The Stoic response to pain for the world has two parts. The first is to distinguish what is in your power: not the outcome of world events, but your kindness, help for those nearby, honesty. The second is not to confuse compassion with endless immersion in the news: that drains you, and the world needs people who still have strength left. You can carry this pain without letting it break you.
world_pain.practice: Choose one concrete good deed within your reach — helping, donating, making a call. Then give yourself an hour without news.

rejection.text: Rejection hurts: a refusal, coldness, a closed door feel like a judgment of your whole self. Epictetus would say that two things are mixed together here: another person's decision, which is not in your power, and your worth, which doesn't depend on it. The Enchiridion (25) has a parable: you weren't invited to the banquet — which means you didn't pay the price it is sold for, flattery and fawning, and you kept what you didn't give away. From the Stoic point of view, someone else's “no” is a fact about their choice, not a verdict on you. That doesn't cancel the pain: the first movements of hurt and sadness are natural. But you don't have to assent to the added judgment “so I'm worth nothing.” Rejection shows how much you wanted connection — and this capacity to reach toward people stays with you.
rejection.practice: Write separately: “what happened” (one sentence) and “what I concluded about myself from it.” Check whether the second really follows from the first.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can run very deep: it seems that without this person your foothold will vanish. The Stoics wouldn't brush this feeling aside, but they would suggest looking gently at where your foothold actually is. Epictetus taught that those close to us are the most precious thing, but not “ours” in the sense of being fully in our power: their decisions belong to them. From this he drew a conclusion that is not cold but freeing: you can love without clutching, and look for support within yourself too — in your capacity to choose, to care, to build connections. Seneca wrote that the wise person is content with himself — and yet still wishes to have a friend (Letter IX). From a Stoic point of view, the fear of losing a bond speaks of its value; at the same time, you can strengthen what doesn't depend on a single person.
abandonment.practice: Name three things that support you apart from this person: an activity, a place, other people. Simply notice that they are there.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is one of the oldest human pains: the feeling is there, but there is no answer. The Stoics wouldn't say you love “in vain.” Love, as they understood it, can be an expression of goodwill, of wishing the other well — and that is a worthy feeling. But they would point to an important distinction: your feeling is yours, you can accept it and give it direction, while the other person's feeling is not in your power. Epictetus considered attempts to control what is beyond our power the chief source of torment. Seneca quotes the Stoic Hecato: “If you would be loved, love” (Letter IX). This is not a promise of reciprocity but a reminder that the capacity to love remains yours. From a Stoic point of view, you can respect your love without demanding an answer from it.
unrequited.practice: Write down what good this love has revealed in you — what qualities, what sensitivity. These qualities will stay with you.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is a burning feeling: it seems your dignity has been taken from you in front of everyone. The Stoics thought about this a great deal, for among them were both the slave Epictetus and the senator Seneca, who lived through exile. Their central idea: dignity is not something that can be taken from outside. The person who humiliated you has command over their own words and actions, but not over whether you agree with their assessment. This doesn't mean they are right or that there is no pain. It means that the last word about your worth remains yours. In On the Constancy of the Wise Man, Seneca wrote that an insult can wound a person, but cannot diminish one whose support lies within. From the Stoic point of view, humiliation says more about the act of the one who humiliated than about you.
humiliation.practice: Say to yourself aloud, or write: “Whatever this person did, my dignity lies in my own actions.” Name one of your actions that you respect.

quote.text: Remember that it is not he who reviles you or strikes you who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting.
quote.author: Epictetus

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is a very common and often quiet pain. The Stoics counted the body among the “indifferents” — that's their term: not something trivial, but something that makes a person neither good nor bad. Among the indifferents there are “preferred” ones — health, strength — but your worth doesn't live there. In Letter LXVI Seneca tells of his friend Claranus, frail and plain in body, and writes that a great and beautiful soul can live in any body and is not diminished by it in the least. From a Stoic point of view, the body is not a shop window for other people's eyes but a companion you can be grateful to for what it does. Standards of beauty change from age to age, but the capacity to be kind and honest stays yours in any body.
body_shame.practice: Name three things your body did for you today: carried you, kept you warm, let you taste something. Simply thank it for that.

illness.text: When your body lets you down, it is frightening and exhausting: plans collapse, and your strength goes into simply getting through the day. The Stoics didn't regard illness as a cause for shame and didn't demand a show of cheerfulness. Epictetus was lame; Seneca was ill a great deal throughout his life and wrote honestly to Lucilius about his ailments. In one letter (LXXVIII) he tells how in illness he was helped by his friends, their care and their conversation, and that a sick person still has important work of their own: not letting fear inflate the suffering, and finding what still brings joy. From the Stoic point of view, illness is neither your fault nor your essence. Your task is not to “defeat” it by willpower, but to find what remains in your power today: attention, a thought, a kind word.
illness.practice: Ask yourself: what is in my power today, however small? Choose one thing — and let the rest not be your job.

quote.text: Disease is an impediment to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses.
quote.author: Epictetus

pride.text: Pride in what you've done is a good feeling, and there's no need to hide it. The Stoics distinguished vanity, which lives on other people's praise, from the eupatheiai — good, rational feelings, among which is calm joy. The joy of a job well done belongs precisely to this realm: it rests not on others' opinion but on your own action. Marcus Aurelius wrote that a person who has done a good deed need not seek witnesses or rewards — like a vine that has borne its grapes and asks for nothing more (V, 6). From a Stoic point of view, healthy pride can be recognized by the fact that it needs no comparison with others and does not fear their indifference. Let yourself feel it: you put your strength and your choice into this.
pride.practice: Write down exactly what you did and which of your qualities went into it — persistence, honesty, care. Stay with it for a minute.

melancholy.text: Bright sadness is a quiet feeling in which sorrow mingles with tenderness toward the world. The Stoics, strangely enough, knew it well. Marcus Aurelius kept returning to the thought that everything flows: people, cities, names give way to one another like leaves the wind scatters on the ground, while spring brings new ones (X, 34). In his hands this sounds not like despair but like an ability to see the beauty of what passes. Seneca wrote that fruit is most welcome when its season is almost over (Letter XII) — and that later years have their own charm. From the Stoic point of view, melancholy can be a kind of clear sight: you see that nothing is eternal, and so your attention to life becomes more tender. There's no need to chase it away; you can give it a little time.
melancholy.practice: Look out the window or step outside for a few minutes and find something that will soon change: the light, the leaves, the clouds. Simply look at it attentively.
